topics.title: What is a cell? The cell theory

learn.hook: Every living thing, from the bacteria in your dahi to a blue whale, is made of cells. It took three scientists and two centuries to say this clearly.
points: The cell is the fundamental structural and functional unit of all living organisms. Unicellular organisms are a single cell that lives independently; multicellular organisms have many cells.
Anton von Leeuwenhoek first saw and described a live cell. Robert Brown later discovered the nucleus.

Matthias Schleiden (1838, botanist) showed that all plants are made of different kinds of cells forming tissues. Theodor Schwann (1839, zoologist) studied animal cells, reported the thin outer layer now called the plasma membrane, and concluded that the cell wall is unique to plant cells. Together they formulated the cell theory.
Their theory did not explain how new cells form. Rudolf Virchow (1855) explained that cells divide and new cells arise from pre-existing cells: Omnis cellula-e cellula.
Modern cell theory: (i) all living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells; (ii) all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

example.q: What did Virchow add to the cell theory of Schleiden and Schwann?
steps: Schleiden and Schwann said organisms are made of cells and cell products.
They could not explain where new cells come from.
Virchow showed new cells arise from pre-existing cells by division.
example.answer: That all cells arise from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula-e cellula).

learn.reallife: Every pathology lab in India, from AIIMS to a district hospital, diagnoses disease by examining cells, a direct use of the cell theory.

topics.title: An overview of the cell: size, shape and parts

learn.hook: The smallest known cell is about 0.3 micrometre long; the largest single cell is an ostrich egg. That is a size range of about five lakh times.
points: Cytoplasm, a semi-fluid matrix, fills the cell and is the main arena of cellular activities. Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus with chromosomes carrying DNA; prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus.
Eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles: ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes, mitochondria, microbodies and vacuoles. Prokaryotic cells lack these.

Ribosomes are non-membrane-bound organelles found in all cells: in the cytoplasm, on rough ER, and inside chloroplasts and mitochondria. Animal cells also have a non-membrane-bound centrosome that helps in cell division.
Size: Mycoplasma about 0.3 µm long; bacteria 3 to 5 µm; human red blood cells about 7.0 µm in diameter; the ostrich egg is the largest isolated single cell; nerve cells are among the longest cells.
Shape varies with function: disc-like, polygonal, columnar, cuboid, thread-like or irregular.

example.q: How many times longer is a 3 µm bacterium than a 0.3 µm Mycoplasma cell?
steps: Divide the bacterium's length by the Mycoplasma's length.

learn.reallife: When blood is tested at a diagnostic lab, technicians check that RBCs are about 7 µm across; abnormal sizes can point to anaemia.

topics.title: Prokaryotic cells: DNA, plasmids and the cell envelope

learn.hook: Antibiotic resistance, one of India's biggest health worries, often travels on tiny rings of extra DNA in bacteria called plasmids.
points: Prokaryotic cells include bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma and PPLO (pleuro-pneumonia-like organisms). They are generally smaller and multiply faster than eukaryotic cells. Shapes: bacillus, coccus, vibrio, spirillum.
All prokaryotes except mycoplasma have a cell wall around the cell membrane. The genetic material is naked, not enclosed by a nuclear membrane: a single circular genomic DNA in the nucleoid.
Many bacteria also have small circular DNA outside the genomic DNA, called plasmids, which give special traits such as resistance to antibiotics.

Cell envelope: a tightly bound three-layered structure: outer glycocalyx, then cell wall, then plasma membrane, working together as one protective unit. The glycocalyx may be a loose slime layer or a thick, tough capsule. The cell wall gives shape and prevents bursting or collapsing; the plasma membrane is semi-permeable.
Based on their cell envelopes and response to Gram's staining, bacteria are Gram-positive (take up the stain) or Gram-negative (do not).

example.q: List the layers of a bacterial cell envelope from outside to inside.
steps: Outermost is the glycocalyx (slime layer or capsule).
Next is the cell wall.
Innermost is the plasma membrane.

topics.title: Mesosomes, flagella, pili, ribosomes and inclusions

learn.hook: A bacterial flagellum spins like a ship's propeller. It has a 'motor' (basal body), a 'joint' (hook) and a long 'blade' (filament).
points: Mesosomes are infoldings of the plasma membrane (vesicles, tubules, lamellae). They help in cell wall formation, DNA replication and distribution to daughter cells, respiration, secretion, and increase membrane surface area and enzyme content. Cyanobacteria have pigment-containing chromatophores.
Motile bacteria have thin filamentous flagella extending from the cell wall. A bacterial flagellum has three parts: filament (longest, outside), hook and basal body.
Pili (elongated tubular structures of a special protein) and fimbriae (small bristle-like fibres) do not help in motility. Fimbriae help some bacteria attach to rocks in streams and to host tissues.
Prokaryotic ribosomes are associated with the plasma membrane, about 15 nm by 20 nm, made of 50S and 30S subunits forming 70S ribosomes. Several ribosomes on one mRNA form a polyribosome (polysome).

Inclusion bodies store reserve material free in the cytoplasm without membranes: phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules and glycogen granules. Gas vacuoles occur in blue-green, purple and green photosynthetic bacteria.

example.q: Name the subunits of a prokaryotic ribosome and its total S value.
steps: Prokaryotic ribosomes have a larger 50S and a smaller 30S subunit.
Together they form the 70S ribosome. (S values are not simply added; 50S + 30S gives 70S.)

topics.title: Eukaryotic cells: plant cell versus animal cell

learn.hook: An onion peel cell and a cheek cell are both eukaryotic, yet one has a wall and a big vacuole, and the other has centrioles. Spot the difference!
points: Eukaryotes include all protists, plants, animals and fungi. Their cytoplasm is extensively compartmentalised by membrane-bound organelles; they have an organised nucleus with a nuclear envelope, complex locomotory and cytoskeletal structures, and genetic material organised into chromosomes.
Plant cells have a cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole, which are absent in animal cells.
Animal cells have centrioles, which are absent in almost all plant cells.
Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic: no nuclear membrane vs true nucleus; no membrane-bound organelles vs many; 70S vs 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes; circular naked DNA vs linear DNA in chromosomes with proteins.

Key labels in diagrams: plant cell (cell wall, plasma membrane, chloroplast, large vacuole, nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi, ER); animal cell (plasma membrane, centrioles, lysosome, nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi, ER).

example.q: A cell has a nuclear envelope, mitochondria, a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole, but no centrioles. What is it?
steps: Nuclear envelope and mitochondria: eukaryotic.

No centrioles also fits a plant cell.

topics.title: The cell membrane: structure and transport

learn.hook: Your RBC membrane is about half protein and half fat, and the proteins drift around like boats on a lake. That's the fluid mosaic model.
points: The membrane is mainly lipids and proteins. Phospholipids form a bilayer with polar heads facing outwards and hydrophobic tails inwards; cholesterol is also present, along with carbohydrates.
The protein-lipid ratio varies; the human RBC membrane has about 52% protein and 40% lipids. Peripheral proteins lie on the surface; integral proteins are partly or totally buried in the membrane.

Fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972): the quasi-fluid lipid lets proteins move laterally. This fluidity is important for cell growth, intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division.

Passive transport needs no energy: simple diffusion of neutral solutes from higher to lower concentration; osmosis is diffusion of water. Polar molecules need carrier proteins to cross the non-polar bilayer.
Active transport moves ions or molecules against the concentration gradient (low to high) using ATP, e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.

example.q: In a human RBC membrane, protein is 52% and lipid 40%. What percentage is left for other components such as carbohydrates?
steps: Total = 100%.
Protein + lipid = 52 + 40 = 92%.
Remaining = 100 - 92 = 8%.

learn.reallife: ORS (oral rehydration solution), promoted in India for diarrhoea, works because glucose and sodium are carried into gut cells together by membrane transport proteins, pulling water in by osmosis.

learn.hook: Your cotton T-shirt is made of almost pure plant cell wall material: cellulose. Cell walls literally clothe India.
points: The cell wall is a non-living rigid outer covering of the plasma membrane in fungi and plants. It gives shape, protects from mechanical damage and infection, helps cell-to-cell interaction and blocks undesirable macromolecules.
Algal cell walls contain cellulose, galactans, mannans and minerals such as calcium carbonate. In other plants, the wall has cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins.
The primary wall of a young plant cell can grow; this capacity diminishes as the cell matures, and a secondary wall is laid on the inner side (towards the membrane).
The middle lamella, mainly calcium pectate, glues neighbouring cells together.
Plasmodesmata traverse the cell wall and middle lamella and connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells.

topics.title: Endomembrane system: ER and Golgi apparatus

learn.hook: Insulin made in your pancreas is built on the rough ER, polished in the Golgi and shipped out in vesicles, like a factory with a packing department.
points: The endomembrane system includes the ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles, whose functions are coordinated. Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are not part of it.

The ER is a network of tubules dividing the cell into luminal (inside ER) and extra-luminal (cytoplasm) compartments. Rough ER (RER) has ribosomes, is common in cells making and secreting proteins, and is continuous with the outer nuclear membrane.
Smooth ER (SER) lacks ribosomes and is the major site of lipid synthesis; in animal cells, steroidal hormones are made in the SER.
Golgi apparatus (Camillo Golgi, 1898): stacks of flat disc-shaped cisternae (0.5 to 1.0 µm across) near the nucleus, with a convex cis (forming) face and a concave trans (maturing) face.

Vesicles from the ER fuse with the cis face and move to the trans face. The Golgi packages materials for targets inside the cell or for secretion, modifies proteins, and is an important site for forming glycoproteins and glycolipids.

example.q: Trace a secretory protein from synthesis to release.
steps: Ribosomes on the RER make the protein.
It is carried in vesicles to the cis face of the Golgi.
It is modified in the cisternae and moves to the trans face.
It is packaged into vesicles and secreted.
example.answer: RER → vesicle → cis Golgi → trans Golgi → secretory vesicle → outside

learn.hook: Amoeba lives in fresh water that keeps flooding in. It survives by pumping water out with a contractile vacuole, like bailing a leaking boat.
points: Lysosomes are membrane-bound vesicles formed by packaging in the Golgi. They are rich in hydrolytic enzymes (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases) that are optimally active at acidic pH and can digest carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

A vacuole is a membrane-bound space containing water, sap, excretory products and materials not useful to the cell. Its single membrane is the tonoplast. In plant cells, vacuoles can occupy up to 90% of cell volume.
In plants the tonoplast moves ions and other materials into the vacuole against their concentration gradients, so their concentration in the vacuole is much higher than in the cytoplasm.
In Amoeba, the contractile vacuole is important for osmoregulation and excretion. In many protists, food vacuoles form by engulfing food particles.
Microbodies are many minute membrane-bound vesicles containing various enzymes, found in both plant and animal cells.

learn.hook: Mitochondria and chloroplasts carry their own DNA and ribosomes, almost like tiny tenants with their own furniture inside your cells.
points: Mitochondria: usually sausage-shaped or cylindrical, about 0.2 to 1.0 µm wide (average 0.5 µm) and 1.0 to 4.1 µm long; number depends on activity. Double membrane: the outer is a continuous boundary; the inner folds into cristae that increase surface area, enclosing the matrix.

Mitochondria are sites of aerobic respiration and make ATP, so they are the 'power houses' of the cell. The matrix has a single circular DNA, a few RNAs, 70S ribosomes and components for protein synthesis. Mitochondria divide by fission.

Plastids occur in all plant cells and in euglenoids. Chloroplasts have chlorophyll and carotenoids for photosynthesis. Chromoplasts have fat-soluble carotenoids (carotene, xanthophylls) giving yellow, orange or red colours. Leucoplasts are colourless storage plastids: amyloplasts (starch, e.g. potato), elaioplasts (oils and fats), aleuroplasts (proteins).

Chloroplasts are found mostly in leaf mesophyll; they are lens-shaped, oval, spherical, discoid or ribbon-like, 5 to 10 µm long and 2 to 4 µm wide. Numbers range from 1 per cell in Chlamydomonas to 20 to 40 per mesophyll cell.

Chloroplast: double membrane (inner less permeable); stroma inside; flattened sacs called thylakoids stacked as grana; stroma lamellae connect grana; thylakoids enclose a lumen and carry chlorophyll. The stroma has enzymes for making carbohydrates and proteins, double-stranded circular DNA and 70S ribosomes.

example.answer: Amyloplasts in potato; chromoplasts in tomato.

topics.title: Ribosomes, cytoskeleton, cilia, flagella and centrioles

learn.hook: Cilia lining your windpipe beat like oars hundreds of times a minute to sweep out dust from Delhi's winter smog.
points: Ribosomes were first observed by George Palade (1953). They are made of RNA and proteins, not surrounded by a membrane. Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S (60S + 40S); prokaryotic are 70S (50S + 30S). S (Svedberg unit) is the sedimentation coefficient, an indirect measure of density and size.
The cytoskeleton is a network of protein filaments (microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments) for mechanical support, motility and maintaining cell shape.

Cilia are small and work like oars to move the cell or surrounding fluid; flagella are longer and move the cell. Their core, the axoneme, has nine doublets of peripheral microtubules and a central pair: the 9+2 array. A central sheath joins each peripheral doublet by a radial spoke (nine spokes); doublets are joined by linkers. Both arise from basal bodies. Bacterial flagella are structurally different.

The centrosome usually has two cylindrical centrioles lying perpendicular to each other, surrounded by amorphous pericentriolar material. Each centriole has a cartwheel organisation of nine evenly spaced peripheral triplet fibrils of tubulin; the central proteinaceous hub is joined to the triplets by radial spokes.
Centrioles form the basal bodies of cilia and flagella, and the spindle fibres that make the spindle apparatus during cell division in animal cells.

example.q: How many microtubules are there in the axoneme of a cilium with the 9+2 arrangement?
steps: Nine peripheral doublets = 9 × 2 = 18 microtubules.

revise.summary: Ribosomes (Palade, 1953) are RNA–protein particles: 80S (60S + 40S) in eukaryotes, 70S (50S + 30S) in prokaryotes. The cytoskeleton gives support, motility and shape. Cilia and flagella have a 9+2 axoneme from basal bodies; centrioles have nine triplets and form spindle fibres.
focus: Ribosome subunits and the S unit
remember: S = Svedberg unit (sedimentation coefficient)
Axoneme: 9 doublets + central pair (9+2) = 20 microtubules
Centriole: 9 triplets of tubulin, cartwheel
traps: Don't give centrioles a 9+2 arrangement; they have 9 triplets
Don't treat S values as simply additive

learn.hook: Each of your cells packs about two metres of DNA into a nucleus a few micrometres wide. That's like stuffing about 20 km of thread into a tennis ball.
points: The nucleus was first described by Robert Brown (1831); Flemming named its stainable material chromatin. The interphase nucleus has chromatin, a nuclear matrix (nucleoplasm) and one or more nucleoli.

The nuclear envelope has two parallel membranes with a perinuclear space (10 to 50 nm). The outer membrane is continuous with the ER and bears ribosomes. Nuclear pores let RNA and proteins move both ways. Mature mammalian RBCs and sieve tube cells lack a nucleus.

The nucleolus is a spherical, non-membrane-bound body, the site of active rRNA synthesis; it is larger and more numerous in cells actively making proteins. Chromatin has DNA, basic histone proteins, non-histone proteins and RNA. A human cell has about 2 m of DNA in 46 (23 pairs) chromosomes.

Each chromosome has a primary constriction, the centromere, with disc-shaped kinetochores on its sides. By centromere position: metacentric (middle, equal arms), sub-metacentric (slightly away from middle, one shorter and one longer arm), acrocentric (close to the end, one very short and one very long arm), telocentric (terminal).
Some chromosomes have a non-staining secondary constriction at a constant location, giving a small fragment called a satellite.

example.q: A chromosome has arms of 2 µm and 8 µm. Where is the centromere and how would you classify it?
steps: The arms are very unequal: one very short, one very long.
So the centromere is close to one end.
This is an acrocentric chromosome.

learn.reallife: Karyotyping labs at AIIMS and other genetic centres look at centromere position and satellites to identify each human chromosome and diagnose disorders.

games.title: Nucleus facts
items: The nucleolus is bounded by a membrane.
The nucleolus is the site of rRNA synthesis.
Active ribosomal RNA synthesis occurs there.
The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with the ER.
Mature RBCs of most mammals have a nucleus.
Kinetochores are on the sides of the centromere.

quiz.q: The site of active ribosomal RNA synthesis is the:
quiz.explain: The nucleolus synthesises rRNA.
steps: The nucleolus is a spherical, non-membrane-bound body.
It is the site of active rRNA synthesis.
Answer: Nucleolus

quiz.q: A chromosome with a terminal centromere is:
quiz.explain: Telo- means end; the centromere is at the tip.
steps: Telo- means end.
A chromosome with a terminal centromere is telocentric.
Answer: Telocentric

quiz.q: A chromosome with the centromere in the middle forming two equal arms is:
quiz.explain: Meta- here means middle.
steps: A centromere in the middle gives two equal arms.
That is a metacentric chromosome.
Answer: Metacentric

quiz.q: The space between the two membranes of the nuclear envelope is the:
quiz.explain: It is 10 to 50 nm wide.
steps: The nuclear envelope has two membranes.
The space between them is the perinuclear space (10 to 50 nm).
Answer: Perinuclear space

quiz.q: Disc-shaped structures on the sides of the centromere are:
quiz.explain: Kinetochores lie on the centromere.
steps: The centromere bears disc-shaped structures on its sides.
These are kinetochores.
Answer: Kinetochores

quiz.q: Which cells lack a nucleus when mature?
quiz.explain: These are NCERT's examples of enucleate cells.
steps: Mature mammalian RBCs and sieve tube cells lack a nucleus.
Answer: Mammalian RBCs and sieve tube cells
options: Mammalian RBCs and sieve tube cells

quiz.q: The non-staining secondary constriction gives some chromosomes a small fragment called a:
quiz.explain: A satellite appears beyond the secondary constriction.
steps: Some chromosomes have a non-staining secondary constriction.
It gives a small fragment called a satellite.
Answer: Satellite

quiz.q: A human cell contains about 2 m of DNA in 46 chromosomes. What is the average DNA length per chromosome, in centimetres?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert metres to centimetres or divides by 92
steps: Answer: 4.35

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What's inside the nucleus, and why do chromosomes look like X, V or J?' Explain!
teach.praise: Chirp! Envelope with pores, nucleolus for rRNA, and chromosomes sorted by centromere. Nucleus mastered!
teach.nudge: Good! What does the nucleolus do, and how are chromosomes classified?

revise.summary: The nucleus (Robert Brown) has chromatin, nucleoplasm, nucleoli and a double nuclear envelope with pores; the outer membrane is continuous with the ER. Chromosomes have a centromere with kinetochores and are metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric or telocentric.
focus: Classification of chromosomes by centromere position
remember: Nucleolus: site of rRNA synthesis
Perinuclear space: 10–50 nm
Metacentric: middle; sub-metacentric: slightly off-middle; acrocentric: near end; telocentric: at end
Enucleate: mature mammalian RBCs, sieve tube cells
traps: Don't call the nucleolus membrane-bound
Don't confuse acrocentric (near end) with telocentric (at end)
